old_entry.title: Ghosts 'n Goblins
old_entry.summary: Ghosts 'n Goblins, known as Makaimura in Japan, is a 1985 platform game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.
body: Ghosts 'n Goblins, known as Makaimura in Japan, is a 1985 platform game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It is the first game in the Ghosts 'n Goblins franchise, and has since been ported to numerous home platforms.

It was a major commercial success across arcades and home systems. It was among the top ten highest-grossing arcade games of 1986 in Japan and the US, as well as the year's sixth best-selling computer game in the UK, with the Nintendo Entertainment System version selling over 1.6 million units worldwide. It initially received generally positive reviews from critics; it is often cited as one of the most difficult games of all time, and has retrospectively been considered one of the greatest video games ever made.

old_entry.title: Commando
old_entry.summary: Commando, released as Senjō no Ōkami in Japan, is a 1985 run and gun video game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.
body: Commando, released as Senjō no Ōkami in Japan, is a 1985 run and gun video game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. The game was designed by Tokuro Fujiwara. It was distributed in North America by Data East, and in Europe by several companies including Capcom, Deith Leisure and Sega, S.A. SONIC. Versions were released for various home computers and video game consoles. It is unrelated to the 1985 film of the same name, which was released six months after the game.

Commando was a critical and commercial success, becoming one of the highest-grossing arcade video games of 1985 and one of the bestselling home video games of 1986. Though not the first military-themed run and gun video game, it spawned numerous clones following its release while popularizing the genre. Its influence can be seen in many shooter games during the late 1980s to early 1990s.

The game later appeared on Capcom Classics Collection, Activision Anthology, and on the Wii Virtual Console Arcade, as well as Capcom Arcade Cabinet for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. A sequel, Mercs, was released in 1989.

old_entry.title: Gradius
old_entry.subtitle: Gradius Turns Power-Ups into Decisions Under Pressure
old_entry.summary: Konami released Gradius in Japanese arcades on May 29, 1985.
body: Konami released Gradius in Japanese arcades on May 29, 1985. The Vic Viper crosses horizontally scrolling stages filled with enemy formations, dangerous terrain and enormous bosses. Its most recognizable innovation is the power-up bar: collecting capsules does not automatically grant a bonus, but moves a cursor among speed, missiles, laser, Option and other capabilities. The player must decide when to spend the resource. Gradius therefore adds a small economic strategy to shooter precision and makes the construction of power part of the tension.

In many shooters, collecting an item produces an immediate effect. Gradius separates collection from activation. Each capsule advances the indicator on the bar, and the player can spend the charge on the current option or wait. The decision is dangerous because delaying an upgrade means facing more enemies with weaker capabilities. The system turns the power-up into a small temporal gamble. Even a seemingly simple resource requires reading the stage, anticipating risk and deciding which form of power is actually needed.

Options follow the Vic Viper's path and reproduce its shots, creating a trail of power the player must learn to position. They are not merely automatic satellites. Because they repeat the ship's previous movement, they can be distributed along trajectories covering different parts of the screen. The system changes the relationship between movement and attack: moving also means drawing where firepower will exist a few seconds later. The ship no longer occupies only one point; it leaves a temporary offensive shape behind it.

Power in Gradius is built gradually, and a death can erase much of what the player accumulated. Restarting in an advanced section with minimal equipment is far harder than arriving prepared. This severity makes each mistake expensive, but also gives successful runs special meaning: the player is not only learning a stage but protecting a configuration built through earlier decisions. Arcade difficulty therefore emerges from the relationship between immediate skill and management of continuity, making survival a form of investment.

old_entry.title: Gyromite
old_entry.subtitle: Gyromite Places a Physical Robot Inside the Game Loop
old_entry.summary: On August 13, 1985 Nintendo released the Gyro Set for the Family Computer Robot in Japan, associated with the game later known in the West as Gyromite.
body: On August 13, 1985 Nintendo released the Gyro Set for the Family Computer Robot in Japan, associated with the game later known in the West as Gyromite. R.O.B. reads light signals from the screen, physically moves spinning gyros and presses controls through a mechanical accessory. The slowness of the process is part of the experience: the player coordinates Professor Hector, the screen and a real object on the floor. It is an unusual interface experiment from before motion, sensors and peripherals became familiar words in console design.

Powered by four AA batteries housed in its hexagonal base, R.O.B. can rotate its torso left and right along five notched positions, move its arms vertically along a central track, and open and close its hands. Compatible games transmit six distinct commands to the robot—move left, move right, move up, move down, open arms, and close arms—by briefly flashing the television screen at a specific frequency. Both Gyromite and Stack-Up include a "Test" utility mode that sends a continuous optical flash to illuminate the red LED indicator on R.O.B.'s head, confirming that the robot's eyes are properly aligned with the television.

When Nintendo of America staff unboxed the first shipment of robots from Japan, their initial excitement over the optical technology was tempered by the hardware's sluggish mechanical speed. Howard Phillips recalled that while the wireless light-sensing concept seemed like "voodoo magic", the robot's physical movement was "hysterically slow". Marketing executive Gail Tilden compared demonstrating the unit in person to "watching grass grow", noting that the robot's optical sensors had to be aligned precisely with the television screen to register the flashes. Product designer Don James remarked that playing Gyromite with R.O.B. was challenging because players had to plan two or three moves ahead to accommodate the robot's turning speed, adding that while the device was novel and enjoyable in short bursts, "like Rock 'Em Sock 'Em Robots, I wouldn't want to do it for 40 hours." Tasked with naming the hardware for North America, Tilden initially considered the name "OTTO" as a play on the word "auto" before settling on "Robotic Operating Buddy", or R.O.B.

The cartridge features three modes: Direct, Game A, and Game B. Direct mode serves as a tutorial that allows the player to send movement commands directly to R.O.B. without playing the main game. In Game A, the player controls Professor Hector with the first controller and presses the Start button to switch control to R.O.B., using the directional pad and the A and B buttons to flash the screen and instruct R.O.B. to pick up a spinning gyro and place it onto the red or blue lever tray. The weight of the spinning gyro holds down the A or B button on the second controller, keeping the corresponding red or blue pillars raised or lowered on screen. In Game B, Professor Hector sleepwalks continuously across 25 stages, and the player controls R.O.B. exclusively without needing to press Start, operating the gates to keep Hector from walking into hazards.

original.old_heading: Gyromite imagines the console as an ecosystem of objects
original.old_body: The game makes full sense only when television, console, robot, gyros and controller are treated as one system. The experiment did not become a standard, but it anticipates a long Nintendo history of peripherals that change play beyond the screen. The narrative works because it is not separated from action. Information, motives and relationships arrive through spaces, systems or behavior, letting what the player understands coincide with what the player is asked to do. A broader principle emerges: the project's identity does not come from one element, but from the way several constraints support one another.
original.heading: Spinning gyros hold the gates open
original.body: The cartridge features three modes: Direct, Game A, and Game B. Direct mode serves as a tutorial that allows the player to send movement commands directly to R.O.B. without playing the main game. In Game A, the player controls Professor Hector with the first controller and presses the Start button to switch control to R.O.B., using the directional pad and the A and B buttons to flash the screen and instruct R.O.B. to pick up a spinning gyro and place it onto the red or blue lever tray. The weight of the spinning gyro holds down the A or B button on the second controller, keeping the corresponding red or blue pillars raised or lowered on screen. In Game B, Professor Hector sleepwalks continuously across 25 stages, and the player controls R.O.B. exclusively without needing to press Start, operating the gates to keep Hector from walking into hazards.

old_entry.title: Gauntlet
old_entry.summary: Gauntlet is a 1985 dungeon crawl maze video game developed and published by Atari Games for arcades.
body: Gauntlet is a 1985 dungeon crawl maze video game developed and published by Atari Games for arcades. It is one of the first multiplayer dungeon crawl arcade games. The core design of Gauntlet comes from the 1983 game Dandy for the Atari 8-bit computers, which resulted in a threat of legal action. It also has similarities to the 1983 maze game Time Bandit.

The arcade version of Gauntlet was released in October 1985, initially available only as a dedicated four-player cabinet. Atari distributed a total of 7,848 arcade units. In Japan, the game was released by Namco in February 1986. Atari later released a two-player cabinet variant in June 1986, aimed at operators who could not afford or did not have sufficient space for the four-player version.

old_entry.title: Karuizawa Yūkai Annai
old_entry.summary: Karuizawa Yūkai Annai is a 1985 adventure game designed by Yuji Horii.
body: Karuizawa Yūkai Annai is a 1985 adventure game designed by Yuji Horii. It was the third and final game in his series of mystery-themed adventure games following The Portopia Serial Murder Case (1983) and Okhotsk ni Kiyu (1984).

Karuizawa Yūkai Annai has players in the role of Shirou Sakaki who is visiting his girlfriend Kumiko Takagi. After Kumiko's sister fails to return from an errand, Shirou and Kumiko go out searching for her.

Karuizawa Yūkai Annai was released for various Japanese personal computers in the mid-1980s and later ported to various feature phones in the 2000s. Unusual for adventure games prior to 1985, the main character speaks in the Karuizawa Yūkai Annai. Horri said that as the game involves an interaction with a girl so he believed that having the playable character talk added more drama and to establish the girl's character. Along with Tokyo Danpa Street which was also published by Enix, it became one the first games to have protagonist characters who would speak spontaneously without interacting with other characters, which would be seen in later Japanese games such as Dōkyūsei (1992) and Yu-no (1996). Karuizawa Yūkai Annai also features some elements of role-playing video games that would appear in his next game Dragon Quest (1986).
